title: Don't be odd
hookLine: philosophy calls for plain living, not a rough robe and unkempt beard to be noticed

cards: Someone starts running, and within a month they own the watch, the shoes, the shorts, the sticker for the car, and they mention their pace at every dinner.
Someone starts meditating and suddenly speaks only in a soft voice and wears linen. A new practice is exciting, and part of us wants to be seen doing it.
Seneca saw the same thing in young Romans who'd just discovered philosophy, and in his fifth letter he gives Lucilius a blunt piece of advice.

teach.b: In Seneca's Rome, some who took up philosophy advertised it. Rough, dirty cloak. Hair uncut, beard untrimmed.
Pointedly refusing silver dishes. Sleeping on the ground where people could see. Don't do any of that to be noticed, Seneca tells Lucilius.
The very name of philosophy already draws enough suspicion without making it ridiculous.
Inwardly, he says, let everything be different. Outwardly, fit in with the people around you. Not a fancy toga, not a filthy one.
Not gold and silver plate, but no need to make a show of avoiding every bit of silver either. The aim is to live better than the crowd, not the opposite of the crowd. Why?
If we look strange, we push away the very people we hoped to help. They'll think that if this is philosophy, they want nothing to do with it.
And deliberately making yourself uncomfortable, to be seen, isn't living according to nature.
Philosophy, as Seneca puts it, asks for plain living, not for punishment.

teach.h: CLAY LIKE SILVER, SILVER LIKE CLAY.
teach.b: Then the line to aim for: admire the person who uses earthenware dishes as if they were silver, and silver as if it were earthenware. Plain without being proud of it. Comfortable without being owned by it.
A practice that needs a costume is partly a performance. The real thing can sit at any table, in ordinary clothes.

how: Many people who practice Stoicism keep their practice quiet and ordinary-looking, aiming to live simply without drawing attention to it.

s: Seneca told philosophers to dress roughly so people would know them
he warns against exactly that: it draws attention and pushes people away.
Seneca says philosophy asks for plain living, not punishment
deliberately making yourself uncomfortable to be seen isn't living by nature.
Seneca wants Lucilius to live the opposite of the crowd
he says to live better than the crowd, not opposite to it.

games.q: you've just fallen in love with philosophy. a friend suggests growing a wild beard and sleeping on the ground so everyone can see. what does Seneca say?
o: yes: show the world you're serious.
no: be different inside, ordinary outside.
games.why: in letter five he says the costume makes philosophy look ridiculous and drives away the very people you hoped to help.

practice: Think of something you practice, a faith, a diet, a workout, a cause, this path, and notice any costume that comes with it: the gear, the special words, the way you bring it up.
No judgment, since everyone has some; just picture a friend who doesn't share it across the table, and notice which piece would make them feel shut out.
Then picture a clay cup and a silver cup side by side, and you using either one the same way, without fuss and without pride.

wordCard.voice: Earthenware. Seneca's fifth letter: admire the person who uses earthenware dishes as if they were silver, and silver as if it were earthenware, plain without being proud of it.

carryVoice: Your line: no costume. Different on the inside, ordinary on the outside, at any table. Day four hundred thirty-seven, done.
